description: We are a team participating in NASA Space Apps from Vitoria da Conquista, Bahia, whose challenge is to present a health monitoring software for astronauts during long-time space missions.
summary: Space-Care is a Body-Area Network (BAN) software with a decentralized, distributed architecture, integrated with NASA’s back-end platform, GHP-IDSP, designed to monitor and guide astronauts in situations that could compromise their physical or psychological health during long-duration space missions. Our solution addresses the challenge because its decentralized architecture ensures data scalability and reliability in low-latency environments. The clinical support provided by the software—covering medical exams, sample collection, and various activities—along with the preliminary analysis of conditions and the gathering of statistics from sensors, enables astronauts to evaluate the best courses of action during the mission to ensure the well-being of the crew.
details:
A pervasive distributed system for health monitoring that incorporates a Body Area Network (BAN), connecting sensors for radiation (dosimeters), heart rate, carbon dioxide (via an acoustic sensor within the spacecraft), and light levels received by the body. This system processes the information through a central hub and transmits it to an available external server.

However, continuous data transmission can lead to information loss and excessive power consumption by the sensors; therefore, data should be transmitted based on specific triggers—such as the detection of anomalies that threaten the well-being of the crew—or at predetermined time intervals.

The software will operate via a decentralized architecture, in which individual servers manage health indicators for a subset of the astronauts. These servers can communicate with one another to request services or information, ultimately generating a comprehensive, global view of the data to be presented to medical personnel. Detailed analysis of the environment in which the astronauts are located (such as a planet or other celestial body), providing data—including gravity and pressure levels—to highlight potential health risks and necessary precautions, such as medical procedures, equipment usage, or the procurement of medication.

Comparison of samples and baseline data collected on Earth with data gathered during the mission to identify changes in the astronaut's health status.

An interface displaying the astronaut’s body, highlighting areas that require closer monitoring (e.g., bones, heart, brain, etc.).

A color-coded system indicating the urgency of medical evaluation for specific body parts: green (low urgency), yellow (moderate), and red (high urgency).

The ability to click on a specific body part to access a detailed report, including the history of previous examinations, recommended follow-up tests, and health metrics (such as heart rate, cell counts, or bone/muscle density).

Suggestions for adjustments to the astronaut’s daily routine—such as modifications to diet, self-care time, physical exercise, or rest periods—based on the collected data.

Identification of the equipment required to perform medical examinations, cross-referenced with the spacecraft’s onboard inventory.

An automated diagnostic assistant to guide astronauts — who are trained to perform self-assessments during the mission— ensuring they follow the correct procedures.

Analysis of saliva samples (liquid or dried) to detect changes in the immune system, specifically assessing the risk of the reactivation of, or exposure to, dormant viruses. (As seen in the "Artemis II" mission, where astronauts provided saliva samples before and after the flight to monitor shifts in immune biomarkers over time.)

Collection of behavioral data to develop a personalized profile for the astronaut regarding health issues that may arise and the measures to be taken by the astronaut throughout the mission.

For the purpose of automation, the system will use previously collected data to draw inferences about factors such as sleep regularity, work overload, and changes in body temperature or heart rate, in order to suggest actions the astronaut can take (such as resting or engaging in self-care).
